p5-elf-b10-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The writer says that “The reason was the seat.” The round door was ground to a taper, “so that pressure from outside drove it further into its seat rather than opening one.” B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what, according to the text, made the round vault door hard to force. The answer must be stated in the text, so look for the reason the writer gives.

steps.title: Set aside two ideas
steps.text: The writer rejects two explanations. The doors went round “not, as the guidebooks like to say, because a circle is the strongest shape.” And weight was not the reason either: “Nor was it a question of mass: the plug doors of that period were often lighter than the slab doors they replaced.”

steps.title: Find the real reason
steps.text: “The reason was the seat.” A square door has corners, and a corner is where a crowbar or a charge of powder “can find a gap to work in”. A round door “was ground to a shallow taper and dropped into a matching taper in the frame”. A taper is a shape that narrows gradually, so pressure from outside pushed the door deeper into its seat instead of opening a gap.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B restates the tapered fit. A makes the door heavier, although the text says the plug doors were often lighter; C brings in a hardened face, which the text never mentions; and D gives the strength of a round shape, the guidebook idea that the writer rejects.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The tapered seat made the door hard to force, not its weight or the strength of a circle. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Vault doors are often pictured as huge and heavy, so weight sounds like the obvious defence.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: “the plug doors of that period were often lighter than the slab doors they replaced”, and “Nor was it a question of mass” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: C uses details that are really in the text: the sixty years, the drill and the 1940s.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions a hardened face. And in the text the drill is not something the round door held off: it is the new threat that ended the round door, “since a drill cares nothing for corners”.

distractors.why_tempting: Many people believe that a circle is the strongest shape, and D explains the round door in that way.
distractors.why_wrong: D argues from the strength of a round shape, the guidebooks’ explanation, which the writer rejects at the start (step 2). Corners do count against the square door in the text, but only because a crowbar or a charge of powder “can find a gap to work in” there, not because a round shape carries load evenly. The reason the writer names is the seat (step 3).

p5-elf-b10-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a text rejects a popular explanation – here with “not, as the guidebooks like to say” – the right answer is the reason the writer gives instead. Look for the sentence that names it, such as “The reason was the seat.”
p5-elf-b10-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: The most familiar explanation is often the trap. D sounds like common knowledge about round shapes, but the writer sets it aside in the very first sentence.

p5-elf-b10-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The usual explanations are the sky and the tiles. At Hallvik “the hall has no windows, the liner is white, and the water is blue anyway”, so neither the sky nor coloured tiles can be the cause. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks why the writer mentions the pool at Hallvik: what job the example does in the text. Look at the sentence where it appears and at the one just before it.

steps.title: Find the usual explanations
steps.text: Just before the example, the writer names the usual explanations of a pool’s blue: “The sky usually gets the credit and the tiling gets the rest”. Tiling means the tiles on the walls and floor of a pool.

steps.title: See what the example removes
steps.text: The pool at Hallvik “settles that question rather neatly: the hall has no windows, the liner is white, and the water is blue anyway.” With no windows there is no sky to reflect, and a white liner – the layer that covers the inside of the pool – gives no colour. The water is still blue, so neither usual explanation can account for it there.

steps.title: Find the real cause
steps.text: The writer then gives the cause: “Water absorbs red light a little more readily than blue, and the effect accumulates”. A white liner “adds no color of its own”; it only sends the light back for a second pass, so the red light has twice as far to travel.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C names the job the example does: the water looks blue with no sky to reflect and no coloured surface to borrow from. A turns the windowless hall into a point about artificial light, B compares a white lining with a blue one, which the text never does, and D puts the colour in something dissolved in the water.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The Hallvik pool shows that a pool of water looks blue even without a sky to reflect or coloured tiles. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A hall with no windows must be lit by lamps, so the example can seem to be about artificial light.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never compares lamplight with daylight, and it never says that daylight washes a tint away. The missing windows matter because they take the sky away (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The white liner is part of the example, and the writer explains what a white liner does.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions a blue lining or says which lining brings out more colour. It says only that a white liner “adds no color of its own” and sends the light back for a second pass (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: Things dissolved in pool water, such as cleaning chemicals, sound like a likely source of colour.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions anything dissolved in the water. It puts the colour in the water itself: “Water absorbs red light a little more readily than blue” (step 4).

p5-elf-b10-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “Why does the writer mention …” questions, look at what comes just before the example. Here the writer names two usual explanations, and the example is built to rule both of them out.
p5-elf-b10-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not take a detail of the example for its point. In the Hallvik example, the missing windows and the white liner matter because they rule out the sky and a coloured surface as the cause.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text keeps returning to one point: the island’s list “is a ratchet” that “registers arrivals and has no way at all of registering departures”. The published figure can only climb, even when the loss “is most of what has happened”. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the right answer must fit all of it, not just one paragraph.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1 introduces Kelvain’s list, which “has never once been shorter than the year before”. Paragraph 2 says that arrivals came as forecast: “New islands are colonized in roughly the order and at roughly the pace the textbooks give.” Paragraph 3 shows how much has left again. Paragraph 4 asks why anything stays. Paragraph 5 ends on Draeven’s remark that “the only number anyone remembers about the place is the one that was never able to fall.”

steps.title: Find the thread
steps.text: A ratchet is a device that can turn only one way. The list adds every new species and has no way to drop one, so “the figure that reaches the newspapers each autumn is a count of everything the island has ever held rather than of anything it holds now.” The same point returns at Odren, whose “published list did not move at all” after the plants its colony had fed thinned by half.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C names this thread. A makes the petrel colony “the one thing” keeping plants alive, B is Ruhe’s view, given in one paragraph, and D says that islands are now reached faster, which the text never says.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about a count that can only rise and so never shows what is lost. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The petrel colony is the most vivid detail in paragraph 4: almost every surviving plant on Kelvain grows under it.
distractors.why_wrong: The colony is one part of the question of why anything stays, not the point of the whole text. And “the one thing … on new volcanic ground” goes too far: the text says that “almost every one of the nineteen surviving plants” on one island grows there.

distractors.why_tempting: Ruhe’s claim is real and memorable: “An island turns to rock in its first winter, or it is a shoal with a name”.
distractors.why_wrong: That is part of Ruhe’s case, given in one paragraph, and it is the part that Draeven grants Ruhe. But the text as a whole is not built around whether islands last; it is built around a count that can only grow (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Species spreading faster than before is a familiar modern story, so it sounds like a likely topic.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says nothing of the kind: islands are colonised “in roughly the order and at roughly the pace the textbooks give” (step 2). It never compares speeds over time or mentions new routes.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: For main-idea questions, look for the idea that comes back in most paragraphs – here the list that can only grow – and choose the option that names it. A vivid detail or one person’s view is usually too narrow.
p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Do not take a quoted person’s view for the main point. Ruhe’s line is the most memorable in the text, but it is given in one paragraph, while the text as a whole keeps returning to a count that can only grow.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: On the question of arrival, Draeven’s surveys “support the textbook almost exactly”: the arrival “sequence held on six of the seven islands, and the totals recorded in the first decade sat close to what had been forecast”. D says the same. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about the arrivals recorded in Draeven’s surveys, so the answer is stated in the text. The arrivals are described in paragraph 2.

steps.title: Find the order
steps.text: “Spores and dust-fine seeds came first, carried on the wind within a season or two of the ground cooling; drift-line plants followed, thrown up on the strandline in mats of weed; the bird-carried species arrived last and slowest.” The strandline is the line on a shore where the sea leaves weed behind.

steps.title: Find how well it held
steps.text: “That sequence held on six of the seven islands, and the totals recorded in the first decade sat close to what had been forecast for ground of that age and that distance from the mainland.” Draeven says that “this part of the record is not in dispute.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches: the expected order on six of seven islands and, in the first decade, totals close to the forecast. A calls the arrivals too irregular to show any order, B puts the bird-carried species ahead of the drift-line plants, and C moves the losses of paragraph 3 into the record of arrivals.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The arrivals came in the expected order on nearly every island and, in the first decade, in about the forecast numbers. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: A sounds scientifically careful, and the order did fail on one of the seven islands.
distractors.why_wrong: The sequence “held on six of the seven islands”, and Draeven says that this part of the record “is not in dispute” (step 3). One exception does not make the record too irregular to read.

distractors.why_tempting: B uses the text’s own terms – bird-carried species, drift-line plants, the seven islands – and its careful wording sounds like the key’s.
distractors.why_wrong: It reverses the order. The drift-line plants came second, and “the bird-carried species arrived last and slowest” (step 2). Since that order held on six of the seven islands, the bird-carried species did not come ahead of the drift-line plants on most of them.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does say that many plants left again, some of them “after a single season”.
distractors.why_wrong: Those losses belong to paragraph 3, not to the record of arrivals. And the text never says that most species were gone by the next survey: the figure it gives is a median stay of “a little over three years” for a wind-arrived plant.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a question names one part of the text – here the arrivals in Draeven’s surveys – find the paragraph about that part and match each option against it. Check the order of events and the numbers word by word.
p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: B is worded as carefully as the key, so a careful tone does not decide. Check the order: in the text the bird-carried species came last.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: “Of the sixty-one plant species on Kelvain's list, nineteen were found in each of the last three surveys.” Nineteen of sixty-one is less than a third. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the plant species recorded on Kelvain. The figures are in paragraph 3.

steps.title: Find the figures
steps.text: “Of the sixty-one plant species on Kelvain's list, nineteen were found in each of the last three surveys. The rest are gone, some of them after a single season”.

steps.title: Do the arithmetic
steps.text: A third of sixty-one is a little over twenty. Nineteen is less than that, so “under a third” is right.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches the figures. B brings in competition between species, which the text never mentions; C turns a median for one group of plants into a fixed term for every species; and D says the count fell, although the list “has never once been shorter than the year before”.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Sixty-one species have been logged, and only nineteen were found in each of the last three surveys. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Newcomers pushing out earlier species is a familiar idea, and the text does say that many early species left.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions competition between species. Where it explains why plants stay on Kelvain, it points to the ground under the petrel colony, “on ground the birds have been manuring for a decade” – fertilising it with their droppings.

distractors.why_tempting: “A little over three years” is a real figure from the text, and C sounds precise.
distractors.why_wrong: The figure is a median – a middle value – and only for one group: “the median stay for a wind-arrived plant on Kelvain works out to a little over three years”. For the fine-seeded composites it is “shorter still”, and some species were gone “after a single season”. So it is not a term that every species keeps.

distractors.why_tempting: Many species left, so it seems natural that the count went down at times.
distractors.why_wrong: The published list “has never once been shorter than the year before” (step 4). And for the plants actually standing, the text says only that the flora “has not grown since about its twelfth year”, not that it fell and recovered.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: When an option turns a figure into a statement, do the arithmetic and check the figure’s scope. Nineteen of sixty-one is under a third, while “a little over three years” is a median for wind-arrived plants only.
p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: The most precise-sounding option is not always right. C sounds exact, but it turns a median for one group of plants into a rule for every species.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Right after “Petrels are also tenants”, the text tells of a colony at Odren that moved after a storm; the plants its nitrogen had fed “thinned by half within four seasons”. Almost all of Kelvain’s surviving plants depend on a colony too, so what survives there is held by birds that could leave. B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the answer is not stated in one sentence; you must join facts. The question gives one fact: almost all of Kelvain’s surviving plants grow under its petrel colony. Petrels are seabirds.

steps.title: Find the Kelvain facts
steps.text: Almost every surviving plant “stands inside the two hectares under the petrel colony, on ground the birds have been manuring for a decade.” The birds’ droppings feed the soil: “Petrels make soil faster than weather does.”

steps.title: Find the Odren episode
steps.text: The next sentence is “Petrels are also tenants.” A tenant lives somewhere without owning it and can move out. At Odren, after a storm took a headland, “the colony there moved to a stack four kilometers away, and the plants its nitrogen had been feeding thinned by half within four seasons.” A stack is a tall pillar of rock standing in the sea.

steps.title: Join the facts
steps.text: The Odren story is the example of birds as tenants. Almost all of Kelvain’s surviving plants depend on a colony too, and a colony can leave. If Kelvain’s colony moved, the plants under it could thin as Odren’s did. The last paragraph adds that an island’s nitrogen usually comes from “a colony of birds with better options elsewhere.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B is the one-step inference: what survives is held there by birds that can go elsewhere. A turns one storm into a rule and the thinning into death, C brings in protection, which the text never discusses, and D says the opposite of what happened at Odren.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Almost all of Kelvain’s surviving plants depend on a colony that could leave. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: A retells the Odren story almost directly, so it feels safe.
distractors.why_wrong: It goes beyond the text twice. The text reports one storm at one cape, not a rule about what storms “will” do, and the plants there “thinned by half within four seasons” – they did not all die (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: If the plants depend on a colony, protecting the colony sounds like a sensible conclusion.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never discusses protecting colonies. What Draeven would like is a change in what is printed beside the arrival list. C takes a step into policy that the text does not take.

distractors.why_tempting: It sounds reasonable that nutrients already in the soil would stay there for a while.
distractors.why_wrong: Odren shows the opposite: after the colony moved, the plants its nitrogen had been feeding “thinned by half within four seasons” (step 3). Losing half of those plants is a real cost, not a small one.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For “suggest” questions, join two facts that the text sets side by side – here Kelvain’s plants under the colony and the Odren colony that moved – and take one small step. Do not stop at retelling one of the facts.
p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: An option that retells a sentence, like A, is not an inference, and it may also stretch the sentence. Here “will” and “to die” both go beyond the text.

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: Draeven “grants him the half of it she thinks is his: nothing colonizes a shoal, and an uncemented island never gets an ecology to lose.” The next sentence, which is given to no one, keeps that point and limits it: “But cementation is a fact about the shore rather than the surface.” Premise allowed, conclusion withheld: that is D. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to Ruhe’s case. Keep three voices apart: Ruhe, Draeven and the writer.

steps.title: Find Ruhe’s case
steps.text: Ruhe “holds that the biology is downstream of the rock and always will be”, that is, life on an island depends on its rock. An island lasts only if its ash sets into palagonite in its first months. In Ruhe’s words: “An island turns to rock in its first winter, or it is a shoal with a name”. A shoal is a shallow place in the sea.

steps.title: Find what is granted
steps.text: Draeven “grants him the half of it she thinks is his: nothing colonizes a shoal, and an uncemented island never gets an ecology to lose.” Uncemented means not set into rock. The writer reports this concession and never questions it.

steps.title: Find what is withheld
steps.text: The next sentence is given to no one, so it is in the writer’s own voice: “But cementation is a fact about the shore rather than the surface.” The “But” keeps the concession and limits it: the rock decides the shore, not the surface. Kelvain’s rim is armoured, but its interior is “still largely bare tephra”, and almost all the surviving plants grow under the petrel colony. So setting into rock is needed for any ecology at all, but it does not settle what grows on the island’s surface.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches. Its first half is a simpler, looser form of the concession – an uncemented island “never gets an ecology to lose” – and its second half withholds Ruhe’s conclusion, that “the rock settles the question”. A gives Ruhe’s view to the writer, B turns a limit into a demolition, and C makes the writer broadly agree with Ruhe.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer accepts Ruhe’s premise but not the conclusion Ruhe draws from it. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Ruhe’s line about the first winter is the most memorable sentence in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: That is Ruhe’s view, in Ruhe’s own words (step 2). The writer limits it at once: cementation “is a fact about the shore rather than the surface” (step 4). And almost all of Kelvain’s surviving plants depend on a colony of birds that could leave, so the island’s future is not fixed in its first winter.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does push back against Ruhe, so a strongly negative option can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: The concession is never taken back: an uncemented island “never gets an ecology to lose” (step 3). The writer limits Ruhe’s case to the shore and never calls it a blind spot or says that the survey record has demolished it.

distractors.why_tempting: C sounds as balanced as the key, and Ruhe is granted part of the case.
distractors.why_wrong: C gets the weight the wrong way round. The bare interior is not a small qualification: with almost all the surviving plants growing under the petrel colony, it is the evidence that the rock does not settle what grows on the island (step 4).

p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For attitude questions, separate what the writer grants from what the writer withholds. Granting a premise – here that an uncemented island gets no ecology – does not mean accepting the conclusion built on it.
p5-elf-b11-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Do not give a quoted person’s words to the writer. Ruhe’s first-winter line is quoted as Ruhe’s, and the writer goes on to limit it.

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The clerk must tell two things apart: a signature written by someone else, or the customer’s own hand “on a bad day”. A signature faked by someone else is a forgery. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “so that a clerk could later judge whether the signature on a cheque was a ___ or merely the same hand on a bad day”. The clerk compares the signature on a cheque with the three on the customer’s card.

steps.title: Find the clue
steps.text: “Whether … or merely the same hand on a bad day” sets two possibilities side by side. One is the real customer writing badly. The other must be a signature written by somebody else, and a signature faked by another person is a forgery. The next paragraph confirms it: it speaks of “the imitator”.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: A mockery is ridicule, or an imitation so poor that it is absurd. Perjury is lying in court after promising to tell the truth. Trickery is the use of tricks in general. None of them names one signature written by someone else.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The clerk had to judge whether the signature “was a forgery or merely the same hand on a bad day”. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: A mockery can be a poor imitation, and a faked signature imitates a real one.
distractors.why_wrong: A mockery is ridicule, or an imitation so poor that it is absurd. The clerk is not judging how absurd a signature looks but who wrote it: someone else, or the customer on a bad day. Only “forgery” names a signature written by someone else (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Perjury is a crime of lying, so it seems to belong with false signatures.
distractors.why_wrong: Perjury is lying in court after promising to tell the truth. A signature on a cheque is not evidence given in court (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Trickery means deceiving people, and a faked signature is a kind of deceit.
distractors.why_wrong: Trickery is deceit in general, the use of tricks. The frame needs a word for one particular signature, set against the customer’s own hand “on a bad day” (step 2).

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a frame offers two possibilities – “whether … or …” – use the one you know to work out the other. Here one is the real customer on a bad day, so the other is a signature by someone else.
p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: All four options have to do with deceit or ridicule, so the general theme does not decide. Ask which word names the thing the clerk is checking: one signature faked by someone else.

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: Copying a signature makes the copyist slow down, so the line goes even, and that evenness showed that the signature had been copied. To expose someone in this way, without their meaning it, is to give them away. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “it was that evenness, more than any tremor of the hand, that ___ the imitator”. The imitator is the person copying someone else’s signature, and a tremor is a shaking of the hand.

steps.title: Follow the reasoning
steps.text: A clerk read habits such as pressure and speed. “Copy those and you must slow down; slow down and the line goes even”. So the even line showed the clerk that the signature was copied. The gap needs a verb for a sign that exposes someone without their meaning it, as in “gave away the imitator”.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: “Gave out” can mean handed out, sent out (a sound, for example) or stopped working, as tired legs give out. “Gave up” can mean stopped trying, or handed someone over, for example to the police. “Gave off” means sent out something such as heat, light, a smell or an air of confidence. None of them fits here: the sentence needs a verb for a sign that exposes someone without their meaning it.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The evenness “gave away the imitator”: it showed that the signature was copied, without the copyist meaning it to. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: All four options are phrasal verbs with “gave”, and “gave out” is one of the most common.
distractors.why_wrong: To give something out is to hand it out or send it out, and when legs or a machine give out, they stop working. None of these fits: the sentence needs a verb for exposing the copyist (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: To give someone up can mean to hand them over to the police, which sounds close to exposing a copyist.
distractors.why_wrong: To give someone up is to hand them over or inform on them on purpose, as when someone gives up a name to the police. The evenness did not hand anyone over or inform on anyone; it was a sign that showed the clerk the signature was copied, without the copyist meaning it to. That is what “gave away” says (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Gave off” can describe signs, as when someone gives off an air of confidence.
distractors.why_wrong: What is given off is sent out, like heat, light, a smell or an air. The evenness did not send the imitator out; it revealed that the signature was copied (step 2).

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: When all four options share a verb, the small word after it decides the meaning. Work out the meaning the sentence needs first – here exposed without meaning to – and then find the phrasal verb that has it.
p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Do not choose by sound. All four are real phrasal verbs, so check each one’s meaning in the sentence.

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The paragraph has just shown the clerks’ method working: the even line exposed the imitator. The gapped sentence turns against that: “none of this amounted to a science”. Nevertheless means in spite of what was just said. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the sentence “___, none of this amounted to a science.” “None of this” points back to the clerks’ method, described just before.

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The sentences before show the method working: the even line exposed the imitator. The gapped sentence says that, all the same, the method was not a science, and the next sentence backs that up with “dozens of disputed cases”. A sentence that holds in spite of what came before needs a word such as “Nevertheless”.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: “Consequently” means as a result, but the method’s success is not the reason it falls short of a science. “Incidentally” means by the way, but this sentence is the paragraph’s main point. “Meanwhile” sets something beside what was just said – another thing happening at the same time, or another side of the situation – but it does not say that something holds in spite of what came before.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Nevertheless, none of this amounted to a science.” The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Consequently” is a common way to draw a conclusion, and the sentence does give a verdict.
distractors.why_wrong: “Consequently” would make the verdict a result of what came before. But the clerks catching imitators is not the reason their method fell short of a science; the verdict holds in spite of that success (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Meanwhile” can set two sides of a situation side by side, which looks like a contrast.
distractors.why_wrong: This sentence is not a second, parallel matter. It is a verdict on the very method just described – “none of this” – and it holds in spite of that method’s success, which is what “Nevertheless” says (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Incidentally” brings in a new point, and the sentence does move on.
distractors.why_wrong: “Incidentally” marks a passing remark. This sentence is the paragraph’s main claim, and the next sentence supports it with “dozens of disputed cases” (step 2).

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: For a connective gap, ask how the gapped sentence relates to the one before. When it states something that holds in spite of what was just shown, choose a word such as “Nevertheless”.
p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Do not pick a connective just because the sentence moves on. Check what “none of this” points back to: the method that the sentences before show working.

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The sentence before grants that the screen is “plainly the better test” on one narrow question. “Yet” then holds back: Solberg will not call the change simply a good one, because something was lost. A change for the better is an improvement. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Yet Solberg declines to call the change a straightforward ___.” The change is the move from paper cards to signatures written on a screen. Straightforward means simple, without complications.

steps.title: Use “Yet”
steps.text: The sentence before says that “on the narrow question of whether two hands are the same hand, it is plainly the better test.” “Yet” turns against that: Solberg will not call the change simply good. The sentences after say what was lost: “The old arrangement asked someone who knew you to vouch for you; the new one asks nothing of anybody”. To vouch for someone is to confirm who they are or that they can be trusted. So the gap needs a word for a change for the better: improvement.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: An impoverishment is a change that makes something poorer. An endorsement is an act of approval, and also a signature on the back of a cheque. An entrenchment is the firm fixing of something already in place. None of them fits “Yet” after “plainly the better test”.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Solberg “declines to call the change a straightforward improvement”: better on one point, but not simply better. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The column spends time on what was lost with the old cards, so a word for loss seems to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: “Yet” must turn against the sentence before, which calls the screen, on one narrow question, “plainly the better test”. Declining to call the change a loss would not turn against that, and the next sentences go on to name what was lost (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: In banking, an endorsement is a signature on the back of a cheque, so the word seems at home here.
distractors.why_wrong: An endorsement is an act of approval. The move from cards to screens is not an act of approval; the sentence weighs whether the change is simply for the better (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Entrenchment” is a formal word for something becoming fixed, and the screen has now taken the cards’ place.
distractors.why_wrong: An entrenchment is the firm fixing of something already in place. The sentence does not ask whether the screen is fixed in place but whether the change is better, as “Yet” after “plainly the better test” shows (step 2).

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a gap follows “Yet”, look at what the sentence before has just granted. Here it grants that, on one narrow question, the screen is the better test, so what Solberg declines to do is call the change simply an improvement.
p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Because the column dwells on what was lost with the old cards, a word for loss can seem right. Follow the logic of “Yet” instead: it turns against “plainly the better test”.

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The scrawl is “illegible, unexamined, demanded all the same”: nobody can read it and nobody checks it, but it is still asked for. Solberg expects it to be demanded long after it has stopped counting for anything. Something that counts for something carries weight. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “demanded all the same, long after it has stopped ___ any weight.” Here “it” means the scrawl that someone drags across a courier’s screen with a fingertip.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: Illegible means impossible to read, and unexamined means that nobody checks it. So the scrawl no longer proves anything, yet it is still demanded. English says that something which has influence, or counts for something, carries weight.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: To shift your weight is to move it, for example from one foot to the other. To gain weight is to get heavier. To pull your weight is to do your fair share of work. None of them means counting for something.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Solberg expects the scrawl to be demanded “long after it has stopped carrying any weight”. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “Shifting” suggests change, and the column is about a change in how signatures are used.
distractors.why_wrong: To shift weight is to move it from one place to another, as when you move your weight from one foot to the other. The sentence is about the scrawl no longer counting for anything (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Gaining weight is a very common phrase.
distractors.why_wrong: To gain weight is to get heavier. The sentence is about a signature that has lost its force, not one that is growing (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Pulling your weight is a well-known expression, so “pulling” sounds natural before “weight”.
distractors.why_wrong: To pull your weight is to do your fair share in a shared task. The point here is not that the scrawl fails to do its share; it is that the scrawl counts for nothing, which is what not carrying any weight means (step 2).

p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: When a gap comes before a noun such as “weight”, test each verb with that noun and ask what the whole phrase means. Only one phrase means having influence, which is what the sentence needs.
p5-elf-b11-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: Each verb forms a real phrase with “weight”, so a familiar sound is not enough. Choose the phrase whose meaning fits: the signature no longer counts for anything.

p5-elf-b11-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: “A falling drop shows only by the light it throws back, and a beam from the front of the house passes straight through the shower and lands on the scenery”. C gives both halves of this reason. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks why, according to the text, stage rain must be lit from the side or from behind. Look for the reason the text gives just before that instruction.

steps.title: Find the problem
steps.text: The water itself is easy: a pipe with the right nozzles “will hang a convincing curtain of it”. “The hard part is being seen.”

steps.title: Find the reason
steps.text: “A falling drop shows only by the light it throws back, and a beam from the front of the house passes straight through the shower and lands on the scenery, which obligingly lights up instead.” The front of the house is where the audience sits. So light from the front lights up the set, not the rain. From the side, or from behind at a shallow angle, “each drop becomes a bright point against a dark ground.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C restates the reason. A says that front light is absorbed, although the text says it passes straight through; B brings in actors’ shadows, which the text never mentions; and D gives the foam a job with light, although the foam deals with noise.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: A drop shows only by the light it returns, and a front beam passes through the rain to the set behind. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: A keeps the text’s idea that a drop shows by the light it throws back, so it sounds close to the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The text does not say that front light is absorbed. It says that a front beam “passes straight through the shower” and lights the scenery, and it never says that the rain would look like a shadow (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Shadows are a real worry in stage lighting, so this sounds like an expert’s reason.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions actors or their shadows. Its reason is that a front beam passes through the rain and lands on the scenery (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The foam in the tray is mentioned right after the lighting.
distractors.why_wrong: The foam belongs to “a separate problem”: it stops “bare metal under a downpour” from drumming loudly enough “to bury the dialogue”. Nothing is said about the foam and light.

p5-elf-b11-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “why” questions, find the reason the text itself gives, often in the sentences right next to the claim. Here a drop “shows only by the light it throws back”, and a front beam “passes straight through the shower”.
p5-elf-b11-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A detail placed near the answer is not always part of it. The foam comes right after the lighting, but it is kept apart as “a separate problem”.

p5-elf-b11-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The devices that work best “take a keeper twenty minutes to prepare each morning”, and the text ends: “The budget line is called enrichment; what it mostly buys is labor.” So the money goes mainly on keepers’ time. B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Imply” means that the answer is not stated outright; you must put sentences together. The question asks about the cost of enrichment. Enrichment means things given to zoo animals to keep their minds and bodies busy, such as puzzle boxes.

steps.title: Find the devices that work
steps.text: The devices that hold attention longest “most resemble the animal's foraging problem in the wild”, and “those are also the ones that take a keeper twenty minutes to prepare each morning.” Foraging is searching for food.

steps.title: Read the last sentence
steps.text: “The budget line is called enrichment; what it mostly buys is labor.” Labour is work, here the keepers’ time. So most of the money pays for the keepers’ work, not for things.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B states this. A brings in prices and what visitors would guess, which the text never mentions; C says that the money goes on other duties, although preparing the devices is enrichment work; and D brings in a comparison with other spending that the text never makes.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The cost of enrichment lies mainly in keepers’ time. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Zoo equipment sounds expensive, and the text does say that enrichment has a budget.
distractors.why_wrong: The text gives no prices and never mentions what visitors guess. It says that the budget “mostly buys” labour, not objects (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The last sentence sounds a little ironic, as if the money were going somewhere it should not.
distractors.why_wrong: The labour in the text is enrichment work: the devices that hold attention longest take a keeper twenty minutes to prepare each morning (step 2). Nothing says that the money goes on ordinary keeping duties.

distractors.why_tempting: Budgets are often defended by comparing costs, so D sounds like a sensible point.
distractors.why_wrong: The text weighs devices against each other – a box that gives up its almonds every time against one that “pays out on perhaps half of all attempts” – but it never sets enrichment against anything else a zoo might fund, or says why enrichment stays in the budget.

p5-elf-b11-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “imply” questions, join the facts the text gives – here the twenty minutes of preparation and the last sentence about labour – and take one small step. Reject options that bring in comparisons or motives the text never mentions.
p5-elf-b11-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: The ironic last sentence can sound like a complaint about money going astray. Read it plainly: the enrichment budget mostly pays for keepers’ work.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: “Ninety-four percent of the street lighting is now full cutoff. The installed output is down about a fifth since the code passed”. Full cutoff means shielded, so that no light goes upwards. C says both things. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about Brackwell’s street lighting since the code of 2016. The figures are in the first paragraph.

steps.title: Find the figures
steps.text: “Ninety-four percent of the street lighting is now full cutoff. The installed output is down about a fifth since the code passed”. The glossary explains that a full-cutoff fixture is built “so that no light leaves it above the horizontal”: it is shielded.

steps.title: Match the wording
steps.text: Ninety-four percent is almost all of the street lighting, and an output that is down about a fifth has come down. A survey plane that flew the valley twice also “measured less light leaving it the second time”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches both figures. A says that the code covers private fixtures, although it governs street lighting only; B says that the audit never established the share, although the share is given to the percent; and D takes the rising uplight from Ashcombe, where no code was adopted, and adds owners who declined to shield, which the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Almost all of Brackwell’s street lighting is shielded, and its total output has fallen. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The sign at the town line says “DARK SKY COMMUNITY”, so the code can sound as if it covers everything.
distractors.why_wrong: The code “governs street lighting”, and the greenhouse at the north edge of town is lit by fixtures that “the code was never written to reach”. The worst single source seen from the dome is “not on a pole”.

distractors.why_tempting: B sounds careful and measured, which can make it seem safe.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: “Every pole in the town has been photographed and logged”, and the share is given exactly – ninety-four percent full cutoff (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does describe uplight – light escaping upwards – rising over the same decade.
distractors.why_wrong: That happened at Ashcombe, “thirty kilometers down the valley”, where “no code was ever adopted”. Brackwell adopted a code, and the text never says that shielding was left to owners.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a question names a place and a time – here Brackwell since 2016 – check that each option is about that place. Wrong options often take a fact from another town or another paragraph.
p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: D borrows one real fact, rising uplight, from Ashcombe, not Brackwell, and adds owners who declined to shield, which the text never mentions. Match the place as well as the facts.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: “Nearly everything they emitted sat inside a band about two nanometers wide, and a piece of glass in front of the detector took that band out of the sky at a cost of well under one percent of the range the observatory works in.” B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about the sodium lamps that Brackwell used before the code. They are described in paragraph 3.

steps.title: Find the description
steps.text: The lamps were “by any ordinary measure, worse”: “They were unshielded, they were orange, and residents complained about them for thirty years.”

steps.title: Find the advantage
steps.text: “But nearly everything they emitted sat inside a band about two nanometers wide, and a piece of glass in front of the detector took that band out of the sky at a cost of well under one percent of the range the observatory works in.” Here a band is a narrow range of colours of light, and two nanometres is very narrow. So a filter could remove nearly all the sodium light and cost the observatory very little.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B matches. A gives a reason for the change that the text never gives, C reverses the comparison of total light, and D turns a cost of “well under one percent” into most of the blue end.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Nearly all the sodium light sat in one narrow band, which a piece of glass could screen out at very little cost to the observatory’s range. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Saving electricity is a common reason for replacing street lamps.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions power. The change came with the code, which is about shielding: the old lamps “were unshielded”, and what replaced them is “shielded”. The only cost the text gives for the sodium lamps is the small part of the observatory’s range that the glass took away (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The ridge lost working nights after the change, so the new lamps can seem brighter.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the reverse: what replaced the sodium lamps is “in total no brighter”, the installed output is “down about a fifth”, and “Fewer photons now arrive at the dome than in the sodium years”.

distractors.why_tempting: D uses the text’s own words about the glass and the range, so it sounds like the price of a filter.
distractors.why_wrong: The cost was “well under one percent of the range the observatory works in”, not most of the blue end (step 3). And the glass blocked the light of the sodium lamps, which “were orange”, not blue.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a text admits that something was worse “by any ordinary measure” and then says “But”, look closely at what follows the “But”. Here it is the narrow band that a filter could remove.
p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: C turns a real comparison the wrong way round. Before choosing, check which period had more light: the new lighting is “in total no brighter”.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: Feltrin “will not credit that to Brackwell”: a recalibration in 2018 and two dry autumns could each “move a three percent figure on its own”. So the improvement cannot be told apart from those other changes. D says this. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the answer is not stated outright. The question asks what the text suggests about the three percent improvement in the zenith reading, the brightness of the sky straight overhead.

steps.title: Find the figure
steps.text: “Across the ten seasons since the code passed, the zenith reading improved by about three percent. Feltrin will not credit that to Brackwell.”

steps.title: Find the reasons
steps.text: “The photometer was recalibrated in 2018, and the two autumns after 2019 were dry enough to leave the valley with less dust in it than the twenty-year average; either of those, she says, would move a three percent figure on its own.” A photometer measures light, and recalibrating it means adjusting it, which can change its readings.

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: If either of two other changes could cause a three percent shift by itself, a three percent improvement cannot be traced to the lighting code. It is too small to separate from the other changes.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D is that inference. A names the recalibration as the cause, which Feltrin does not do; B gives the code credit that Feltrin withholds; and C condemns this kind of monitoring in general.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The improvement is too small to tell apart from the other changes of those years. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: The recalibration is one of the two possible causes named in the text, so A seems to follow.
distractors.why_wrong: Feltrin says that “either of those” – the recalibration or the dry autumns – could move the figure on its own, not that the recalibration did. A picks one cause where two are left open (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The street lighting was shielded and its output fell, and paragraph 3 links “a slightly better zenith number” to fewer photons arriving at the dome. B also sounds modest.
distractors.why_wrong: Feltrin “will not credit that to Brackwell” (step 2): a recalibration or two dry autumns could each move a figure that small (step 3). And B’s second half, “by less than the shielding work would suggest”, is a comparison that appears nowhere in the text.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does show that one reading cannot settle the question here.
distractors.why_wrong: C goes much further. Feltrin’s doubt is about one small figure, and Feltrin relies on another series from the same observatory: the nights on which the faint-galaxy programme reached its target.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: For “suggest” questions about a figure, look at what could have caused it. When more than one cause could explain the figure on its own, the figure cannot be credited to any one of them.
p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Do not pick one of the possible causes as the answer. Two are named, and either could do it alone, so neither is shown to be the cause.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Feltrin grants Rieger “the half she thinks is his”, and the next sentence, given to no one, states it flatly: “Where the fixtures are unshielded the fixtures are the story.” But the worst single source seen from the dome “is not on a pole”, so what is left after shielding is not just “corrections on corrections”. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to Rieger’s case. Keep the voices apart: Rieger, Feltrin and the writer.

steps.title: Find Rieger’s case
steps.text: Rieger says that uplight from unshielded fixtures “is the dominant term in any sky-glow budget by a wide margin; fix that and what is left are corrections on corrections.” Uplight is light that escapes upwards, and the dominant term is the biggest part. So, for Rieger, once fixtures are shielded, whatever is left hardly matters.

steps.title: Find what is granted
steps.text: Feltrin “grants him the half she thinks is his, and grants it without hedging”: at Ashcombe, where no code was adopted, “every number the ridge keeps got worse together.” The next sentence is given to no one, so it is the writer’s own: “Where the fixtures are unshielded the fixtures are the story.”

steps.title: Find what is refused
steps.text: “But Brackwell's code governs street lighting, and the worst single source now visible from the dome is not on a pole.” The paragraph goes on to a greenhouse lit through the winter nights, which the code “was never written to reach”. Paragraph 3 adds that the new white street light cannot be filtered out: “There is no filter for white.” So what is left after shielding is more than a small correction.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A matches: the point is granted where fixtures are unshielded, but not the verdict on what is left over. B gives Rieger’s telescope-time line to the writer, C turns a limit into a dismissal, and D makes the greenhouse a minor exception.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer grants Rieger’s point about unshielded fixtures, but not the verdict on what is left. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: “It is not obliged to buy telescope time” is one of the most quotable lines in the text, and Feltrin says that Brackwell “did what it was asked to do”.
distractors.why_wrong: That line is Rieger’s, given in Rieger’s own voice. The writer never adopts it; the paragraph goes on to a large source of light that shielding does not deal with (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: The writer does disagree with part of Rieger’s case, so a strongly negative option can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: Feltrin makes the concession “without hedging”, and the writer’s own next sentence states it flatly: “Where the fixtures are unshielded the fixtures are the story.” The record at Ashcombe supports Rieger there (step 3). The writer never calls the model an evasion or says that it has been discredited.

distractors.why_tempting: D sounds as balanced as the key, and Brackwell did shield ninety-four percent of its street lighting.
distractors.why_wrong: D gets the weight wrong. The paragraph says that “the worst single source now visible from the dome is not on a pole”, and it then turns to the greenhouse. That is no minor exception; together with the white street light that cannot be filtered, it is why Rieger’s account does not settle things at Brackwell (step 4).

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For attitude questions, find what is granted and what is refused. Here the point about unshielded fixtures is granted, but not the claim that everything left over is a small correction.
p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Two options sound measured. A and D both grant Rieger something, but D makes the greenhouse minor, while the worst single source seen from the dome is not on a pole. Check the weight as well as the tone.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: Brackwell judges its lighting by counting poles and fixture types; the observatory measures the light that reaches it. The text ends: “The units were poles. The ridge counts photons, and for ten seasons the two records were not describing the same valley.” C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the answer must fit all of it.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1 gives Brackwell’s record: every pole logged, ninety-four percent full cutoff. Paragraph 2 sets Feltrin’s record at the observatory against it: the target nights fell from sixty-one to thirty-eight. Paragraph 3 explains how less light can still cost nights: “There is no filter for white.” Paragraph 4 gives Rieger’s case and the greenhouse that the code does not reach. Paragraph 5 sets the two records side by side.

steps.title: Find the thread
steps.text: The last paragraph names it: “The units were poles. The ridge counts photons, and for ten seasons the two records were not describing the same valley.” Photons are the tiny particles that light is made of. The town counts fixtures; the observatory measures what reaches the dome.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C names this thread. A brings in population growth, which the text never mentions; B makes the greenhouse “the one thing”, although the white street light also costs nights; and D says that total light rose, although fewer photons now reach the dome.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about a count of fixtures that does not match the light reaching the dome. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Growing towns are a common cause of brighter skies, and the ridge did lose nights over the decade.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions population. And the light did not grow: Brackwell’s installed output is “down about a fifth”, and a survey plane that flew the valley twice “measured less light leaving it the second time”.

distractors.why_tempting: The greenhouse is the most vivid detail in the text, and it is lit through the winter nights.
distractors.why_wrong: It is one part of the argument, and “the one thing” goes too far. Paragraph 3 gives a second cause: the new white street light cannot be filtered out, because “There is no filter for white.”

distractors.why_tempting: The observatory did lose nights, from sixty-one to thirty-eight, so rising light seems to explain it.
distractors.why_wrong: Total light fell: “Fewer photons now arrive at the dome than in the sodium years”. The nights were lost because “a smaller share of the sky can be kept clear of them”.

p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For main-idea questions, read the last paragraph closely: it often names the thread that runs through the text. Here it sets the town’s count of poles against the observatory’s count of photons.
p5-elf-b12-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: A vivid detail, such as the greenhouse, is rarely the main point. Check whether an option with “the one thing” leaves out other causes the text gives.

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Few of the volunteers could say what they had just agreed to. To describe or report something is to give an account of it, so “give any account of” fits. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “few of her volunteers could give any ___ of what they had just agreed to”. The volunteers had spent a median of eleven seconds on the terms and conditions.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The sentence means that few of them could say what the terms contained. To describe or report something is to give an account of it, so “could give any account of what they had just agreed to” fits.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: An accord is a formal agreement between two sides. A discount is a cut in price. As a noun, a recount is usually a second count, for example of the votes in an election. Only “account” fits the frame: “give any account of” means describe or report.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Few of her volunteers could give any account of what they had just agreed to”. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph is about agreeing to terms, and an accord is an agreement.
distractors.why_wrong: An accord is an agreement between two sides, such as two countries. The sentence is about whether the volunteers could describe the terms, not about reaching an agreement (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The volunteers were signing up to a music app, and a discount belongs to buying and selling.
distractors.why_wrong: A discount is a cut in price. The sentence is about what the volunteers could say about the terms, not about prices (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The verb recount can mean to tell a story, which sounds close to describing.
distractors.why_wrong: After “any” the gap needs a noun. As a noun, a recount is usually a second count, for example of votes. The noun that fits is “account”: to give an account of something is to describe or report it (step 2).

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap sits between a verb and “of”, think of the expressions that use that verb – here “give any account of”, meaning describe. Then check that the meaning fits the sentence.
p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: “Accord” is tempting because the paragraph is about agreeing. A word that matches the topic is not enough; it must fit the expression and the meaning.

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The gapped sentence gives the obvious explanation, length, before the paragraph tests it with “But her second experiment …”. A word meaning as one would expect fits: “Naturally”. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the paragraph: “___, the usual explanation blames length.” The document ran to nine thousand words, which would take a reader at an ordinary pace “the better part of an hour”.

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The gapped sentence states the usual, expected explanation. The paragraph then tests it: “But her second experiment suggests that brevity alone is far from ___.” So the gap needs a word that grants the expected view before the “But” comes. “Naturally” means as one would expect.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: “Consequently” means as a result, but the usual explanation is not a result of the sentence before. “Conversely” would present the sentence as the reverse of the one before, but blaming length reverses nothing there. “Ultimately” means in the end, but length is where the argument starts, not its final point.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Naturally, the usual explanation blames length.” The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: “Consequently” is a common link between sentences, and the paragraph does go on to explain.
distractors.why_wrong: It would make the usual explanation a result of the volunteers’ judgement that reading would have changed nothing. It is not a result; it is the expected view that the paragraph goes on to test (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The paragraph does contain a contrast, so a contrast word seems to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: “Conversely” would present this sentence as the reverse of the one before. Blaming length does not reverse anything there; the contrast comes two sentences later, with “But her second experiment …” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Ultimately” sounds weighty, and the paragraph is reaching a judgement.
distractors.why_wrong: “Ultimately” marks a final point. The length explanation is where the paragraph starts: the view that it goes on to question (step 2).

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a sentence states the usual view and the paragraph then turns with “But”, the gap before the usual view often needs a word that grants it, such as “Naturally”.
p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Do not put the contrast in the wrong place. The turn comes two sentences later, with “But”; the gapped sentence only sets up the expected view.

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: “Far from” means not at all. Shortening the terms to one page did not make people read them, so brevity alone does not settle the matter: it is “far from decisive”. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “But her second experiment suggests that brevity alone is far from ___.” Brevity means shortness.

steps.title: Use “far from”
steps.text: “Far from” means not at all, so the gap names what brevity is not. The evidence follows: on a single page of plain language the median rose to twenty-two seconds, and “People still did not read them.” So shortness alone does not decide whether people read: it is far from decisive.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: “Far from ineffective” would mean that brevity worked well, the opposite of the result. “Far from excessive” would mean that the brevity was not too great, which is not the question. “Far from dismissive” would say that brevity does not brush the matter aside, which has nothing to do with whether people read the terms.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Brevity alone “is far from decisive”. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: The volunteers brushed the terms aside, so a word for brushing something aside seems to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: Dismissive describes someone, or something they say, that treats a matter as unimportant. “Far from dismissive” would say that brevity does not brush the matter aside, which has nothing to do with whether people read the terms (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The first document was very long, so a word about too much seems to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: “Far from excessive” would say that the brevity was not too great. The experiment asks whether shortness makes people read, not whether the page was too short (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The result was disappointing, so a negative-sounding word seems to match.
distractors.why_wrong: “Far from” turns the word round: “far from ineffective” would mean that brevity worked well. But people “still did not read them” (step 2).

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a gap follows “far from”, the gap names the opposite of what is true. Decide what the evidence shows first, then choose the word that “far from” turns into that meaning.
p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: The disappointing result pulls towards the negative word, “ineffective”. But “far from” reverses it, so check the whole phrase against the evidence.

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: Clicking is “not to strike a bargain but to ___ that there was never one to strike”: the user admits a fact, that no bargain was possible. To admit something, often unwillingly, is to concede it. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “To click, in those circumstances, is not to strike a bargain but to ___ that there was never one to strike.” To strike a bargain is to make a deal.

steps.title: Find the meaning
steps.text: “No private person has ever negotiated a clause of such a document”, and “the choice on offer is the whole of it or none of the service”. So clicking does not make a deal; it admits a fact, that a deal was never possible. To admit something, often unwillingly, is to concede it, and “concede that …” is followed by the fact admitted.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: To accede is to agree to a request or a demand. To precede is to come before something. To recede is to move back or to grow fainter. None of them means admitting a fact.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Clicking is “not to strike a bargain but to concede that there was never one to strike”. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: To accede means to agree, and clicking looks like agreeing to the terms.
distractors.why_wrong: To accede is to agree to a request or a demand. What follows the gap is not a request but a fact – that there was never a bargain to strike – and the click admits it (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Precede” looks and sounds very like the key.
distractors.why_wrong: To precede is to come before something in time or order. The click does not come before a fact; it admits one (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The passage is about choice being emptied out, and recede suggests something fading away.
distractors.why_wrong: To recede is to move back or to grow fainter. The click does not move back or fade; it admits a fact (step 2).

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: When four options look alike, as these -cede verbs do, put each one into the sentence and ask what it would mean there. Here only one means admitting a fact.
p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: “Accede” is tempting because clicking seems like agreeing. But the frame sets making a bargain against admitting that there was none to make.

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The words after the dash explain the gap: “a gesture that preserves the form of choice while quietly emptying it of content.” Something done only for the sake of form, with no real meaning, is a formality. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “is not a considered agreement at all but a ___ — a gesture that preserves the form of choice while quietly emptying it of content.” A considered agreement is one made after thinking it over.

steps.title: Use the words after the dash
steps.text: The part after the dash defines the gap: the click keeps “the form of choice” but empties it “of content”. A formality is something done only because a procedure requires it, not because it decides anything. That is exactly such an empty gesture.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: Finality is the quality of being final and settled. Neutrality is not taking sides. A banality is something dull and unoriginal, often a remark. None of them is an empty gesture that keeps only the form of something.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Consent on those terms, Hallenbeck argues, is “not a considered agreement at all but a formality”. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Clicking ends the sign-up, so a word for something being final seems to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: Finality is the quality of being final and settled. The words after the dash describe something else: a gesture that keeps “the form of choice” while emptying it “of content”. That is a formality, not finality (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Neutrality” sounds suitably formal for an argument about law.
distractors.why_wrong: Neutrality is not taking sides. The sentence is about a gesture that keeps the form of a choice but has no content, not about taking sides (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Clicking to accept terms is an everyday routine, and a banality is something commonplace.
distractors.why_wrong: A banality is something dull and unoriginal, often a remark. Being dull is not the point here: the words after the dash describe a gesture that keeps the form of choice while emptying it of content (step 2).

p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: When a dash follows the gap, read what comes after it: it often explains the missing word. Here “a gesture that preserves the form of choice” describes a formality.
p5-elf-b12-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: All four options end in -ality, so the look of the word does not help. Use the explanation after the dash.

p5-elf-b12-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: “The rule is that a handle must not be checkable”: a name like Ferrymouth Haze “cannot be held up beside a ferrymouth haze and found wrong”, while a customer can catch out a name like Tomato. B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the rule used to name a shade. The rule is stated directly in the text.

steps.title: Find the rule
steps.text: The trade calls paint names handles. “The rule is that a handle must not be checkable.” Checkable means that someone could test it against the real thing, and so could find it wrong.

steps.title: Follow the example
steps.text: “Ferrymouth Haze cannot be held up beside a ferrymouth haze and found wrong; Tomato can, and a customer who grows tomatoes will say so at the counter.” So the winning names “drift toward places nobody has been and weather nobody has photographed”: names that no customer can prove wrong.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B states the rule. A turns the reason why an occasional exception survives into the rule, C is the opposite of the rule, and D brings in colour standards, which the text never mentions.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: A name is chosen so that no customer can show it to be wrong. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does say that a name can borrow from something that “comes in enough versions to swallow the error”.
distractors.why_wrong: That is said only of “The occasional literal name”, such as brick, ash and sand – the reason a rare exception survives. The rule itself is that a handle “must not be checkable” (step 2). And many versions matter only because they make a literal name impossible to check: there are “enough versions to swallow the error”.

distractors.why_tempting: Most people expect a paint name to describe its colour.
distractors.why_wrong: The text opens by saying that “the names are not descriptions”, and the rule works the other way: a name that can be checked against the real thing, like Tomato, can be found wrong (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: D mentions “the trade”, a phrase the text also uses.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions colour standards. The test in the text is whether a customer can catch a name out, “at the counter” (step 3).

p5-elf-b12-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a short text states a rule and then gives examples, the examples show what the rule means. Match the options against the rule, not against an exception mentioned later.
p5-elf-b12-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: An exception is not the rule. The literal names brick, ash and sand are mentioned only to explain why the occasional literal name survives.

p5-elf-b12-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Steinvik says that “two balls lifted from the same box can differ more, in the tunnel, than two rival designs differ on paper.” So the difference between advertised patterns can be smaller than the variation within one box. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that the answer is not stated word for word; you must work it out. The question asks about the dimple patterns that makers advertise. Dimples are the small hollows on the surface of the ball.

steps.title: Find what the tunnel shows
steps.text: “Depth is what the tunnel notices”: a dimple “shallower by twelve microns behaves almost like no dimple at all”, and twelve microns “is inside the drift of a mould across a single production run.” A micron is a thousandth of a millimetre, and the drift of a mould is the small change in it as it is used again and again.

steps.title: Find the comparison
steps.text: Steinvik says that “two balls lifted from the same box can differ more, in the tunnel, than two rival designs differ on paper.” Rival designs are the patterns of competing makers. So the difference between two advertised patterns can be smaller than the variation between balls from one box.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C states this inference. A gives a rule about deeper dimples that the text never gives, B invents a reason for choosing patterns, and D says that the arrangement has no bearing, which Steinvik will not say.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Rival patterns can differ less than two balls from the same box. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Depth is what matters in the tunnel, so a rule about deeper dimples seems to follow.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says only that a dimple twelve microns too shallow “behaves almost like no dimple at all” (step 2). It never says that deeper dimples give a longer flight, and A says nothing about the advertised patterns, which the question asks about.

distractors.why_tempting: The mould is mentioned in the text, so B seems connected to it.
distractors.why_wrong: The mould comes up only as the source of drift in depth across a production run (step 2). The text never says how makers choose their patterns.

distractors.why_tempting: The patterns “matter less than the catalogues suggest”, so it is easy to go one step further.
distractors.why_wrong: Steinvik “will not go so far as to call the arrangements decorative”, and thinks that hexagonal packing “does buy a little” at the margins. So, in Steinvik’s view, the arrangement has some bearing, if a small one.

p5-elf-b12-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “implied” questions, look for a comparison and take one small step from it. Here two balls from one box can differ more than two rival designs.
p5-elf-b12-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Watch for an option that goes one step too far. The patterns matter less than advertised, which does not mean that they do not matter at all.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The cooperative “registered the Aveste mark in 2014”, the mark “is precise about equipment” and “bars washing”, and the cooperative holds 212 of the 340 pans, a little under two thirds. D puts these facts together. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the Aveste mark, the protected name for the salt. The facts are in paragraph 1.

steps.title: Find the facts
steps.text: “Two hundred and twelve of the pans belong to the cooperative that registered the Aveste mark in 2014; the rest are worked by two families who never joined and sell under no name at all.” There are three hundred and forty pans in all, and the two families sell under no name, so the mark can only cover the cooperative’s 212 pans.

steps.title: Find what the mark sets out
steps.text: “The mark is precise about equipment. It names the lath, keeps metal out of the pan, bars washing and heat-drying, and sets out how the sheds are ventilated.” A lath is a thin strip of wood, used here to rake out the salt.

steps.title: Check the figure
steps.text: Two thirds of 340 is about 227, so 212 is a little under two thirds. “About two thirds” is a rounded figure.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches all three facts. A says that the mark governs every pan, B says that its methods were never written down, and C gives a reason for the registration that the text never gives.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The mark, registered in 2014, fixes the equipment, bars washing and covers about two thirds of the pans. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Salt that carries the mark fetches about six times the price of industrial salt, and a name that covers a whole place sounds natural.
distractors.why_wrong: Only 212 of the 340 pans belong to the cooperative; the rest are worked by two families who “sell under no name at all” (step 2). And the text gives no reason for the price.

distractors.why_tempting: Craft rules are often vague, and Solbes spends five seasons trying to find out which of the rules really matter.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite: “The mark is precise about equipment”, and it lists what the mark names and bars (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Protecting a place name from imitators is a common reason for registering a mark.
