distractors.why_wrong: The text never says why the mark was registered, and it never mentions producers on other coasts or anyone else selling salt under the Aveste name. Panek calls a mark “an instrument against fraud”, but that is Panek’s view of what a mark is for, not a reason given for this registration.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: When an option gives a figure, find the figure in the text and check it. Here 212 of 340 pans is a little under two thirds, so “about two thirds” holds.
p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A reason that sounds normal in the real world, like C’s, is a trap if the text never gives it. Only what the text says counts.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: Pella Marsa “was floored in the 1990s to take a small harvester, and its dates are settled before the season opens”. A says both things. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about the saltern at Pella Marsa. A saltern is a chain of shallow ponds in which sea water is dried to salt, as the glossary explains. Pella Marsa comes up in paragraph 3.

steps.title: Find the description
steps.text: “The saltern at Pella Marsa, forty kilometres up the coast, was floored in the 1990s to take a small harvester, and its dates are settled before the season opens, because the contractor who owns the machine works six sites between March and September.” And: “The brine there stands as long as the calendar says it stands.”

steps.title: Find why its salt stands out
steps.text: Solbes’s panels can pick its salt out, but “it is not that the harvester bruises the crystal. It is that the harvester comes on a Tuesday.” The salt is lifted on a fixed day, not on the day the crust is ready.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A restates the floors and the fixed dates. B gives the reason that the text rules out, C describes the two families at Aveste, and D brings in washing and grading, which the text never mentions for Pella Marsa.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Pella Marsa’s floors were laid for a machine, and its dates are fixed in advance. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: The panels can pick Pella Marsa out, and a machine damaging the salt sounds like the obvious reason.
distractors.why_wrong: The text rules this out: “it is not that the harvester bruises the crystal. It is that the harvester comes on a Tuesday.” Nor does it say that the salt was told apart “in every trial” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Two families who sell under no name do appear in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: Those families work pans on the Aveste flats, not at Pella Marsa: of the 340 Aveste pans, “the rest are worked by two families who never joined and sell under no name at all”.

distractors.why_tempting: Aveste salt is “sold unwashed”, so it seems natural that the machine-harvested salt is washed.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says what happens to Pella Marsa’s salt after it is lifted. What sets it apart, in the text, is timing: “the harvester comes on a Tuesday” (step 3).

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: When a text describes several places, check that each option is about the place the question names. Wrong options often borrow a true detail from another place.
p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: B gives the reason most readers would guess, a machine bruising the salt, but the text says outright that this is not the reason. Read on after “pick Pella Marsa out”: the same sentence says “it is not that the harvester bruises the crystal”.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: “On chemistry the three relined pans behave like the clay ones”, but the pair who worked them misread the crust on the new floors for two seasons. The paragraph ends: “Nothing her panels could find in the salt recorded the relining. The people did.” B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that you must put facts together. The question asks about the three pans that were given new concrete floors in 2019.

steps.title: Find the chemistry
steps.text: “On chemistry the three relined pans behave like the clay ones.” In paragraph 2 the tasting panels found no difference either: clay came out level against “the three pans relined with concrete in 2019”.

steps.title: Find what changed
steps.text: “But concrete dries faster at the edges, and the pair who worked those pans in 2019 and 2020 misread the crust in both seasons and lifted late”. Then: “By 2021 they had the new floors by heart and the lateness stopped.” The crust is the layer of salt that forms in the pan, and reading it means judging when it is ready to lift.

steps.title: Join the facts
steps.text: So the new floors changed how the crust had to be read, not what was in the salt. The paragraph ends on this point: “Nothing her panels could find in the salt recorded the relining. The people did.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B states this. A turns the chemistry result into a rule about cost, C raises a doubt about the mark that the text never raises, and D says that the concrete pans gave more magnesium, which the chemistry result denies.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The relining showed up in how the pans had to be read, not in the salt. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The salt from concrete and clay did come out the same, so the floor may seem not to matter.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never discusses the cost of floors, and the new floors did matter: the pair who worked those pans misread the crust “in both seasons and lifted late” until they knew the floors by heart (step 3). A takes a step that the text does not take.

distractors.why_tempting: The mark has strict rules about equipment, and the relined pans caused problems.
distractors.why_wrong: The late seasons were about timing, and they ended: “By 2021 they had the new floors by heart and the lateness stopped” (step 3). Nothing in the text says that those two seasons raise any doubt about whether concrete pans can meet the mark.

distractors.why_tempting: D uses the text’s own words, “dries faster at the edges”, and the text does link magnesium with time in the pond.
distractors.why_wrong: “On chemistry the three relined pans behave like the clay ones” (step 2). What faster drying changed was how the crust had to be read (step 3), not what was in the salt.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: For “implied” questions, look for two facts set against each other – here the same chemistry but two misread seasons – and say what follows from both. A short closing line such as “The people did.” often states the point.
p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: D sounds scientific and reuses the text’s words, but it contradicts the chemistry result. Check every claim in an option against the text.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The writer reports Panek’s objection without criticism and says of the inspector’s problem that “nobody has answered that yet”. But the last sentence still sets the guaranteed lath, “which no panel in five seasons has managed to taste”, against the morning judgement “which every panel can taste”. A fair objection, but not the end of the argument: that is C. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to Panek’s objection. Keep the voices apart: Panek, Solbes and the writer.

steps.title: Find the objection
steps.text: Panek “has read all of it and disputes none of it. His objection is procedural.” In Panek’s words: “You can photograph a lath” but “You cannot photograph a decision about whether the crust is ready.” On Panek’s account, a mark is a tool against fraud, and it must hold up for an inspector who arrives unannounced.

steps.title: See how the writer treats it
steps.text: The writer reports the objection without criticism and adds that Solbes “agrees with every word of that”. In the last paragraph the committee asks how an inspector arriving on a Thursday could check a number that was true only on Tuesday morning, and the writer notes that “nobody has answered that yet.” So the objection stands as a real difficulty.

steps.title: See what it does not settle
steps.text: The last sentence sets two things side by side: the mark goes on guaranteeing “a wooden lath, which no panel in five seasons has managed to taste”, while the morning decision at the last pond is something “every panel can taste, and nothing at Aveste writes that part down.” The case for recording dwell – the days the brine stands in the final pond before the salt is lifted – is left open.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches: the objection is treated as fair, but it does not close the argument. A gives Panek’s view to the writer, B invents a motive for the committee, and D says that Solbes answered Panek, although Solbes agrees with Panek.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer allows that the objection is fair but does not let it end the argument. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The writer reports Panek’s view at length and never argues with it directly.
distractors.why_wrong: That a mark is “an instrument against fraud rather than a description of a craft” is Panek’s account (step 2). The writer does not leave the craft question there: the last sentence sets the lath that no panel in five seasons has managed to taste against the morning judgement that every panel can taste (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: Solbes’s request has not been granted, so a reluctant committee may seem to be the story.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests bad faith. The committee “has not refused it either”; it has asked a real question that “nobody has answered” yet (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: D sounds balanced, and Solbes does go on to point to the concrete pans.
distractors.why_wrong: Solbes does not answer Panek’s objection; Solbes “agrees with every word of that” (step 3) and then adds a further point about the concrete pans. And the inspector’s visit is not a small leftover: how an inspector could check the dwell is the very question that nobody has answered.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: For attitude questions, check how the writer treats an objection: whether it is reported fairly, and whether it is allowed to settle the matter. A fair objection can still leave the argument open.
p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Do not give the writer a quoted person’s view because the writer reports it at length. Panek’s account of what a mark is for stays Panek’s.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The mark protects tools such as the lath, which an inspector can check. But the panels show that the salt depends on dwell – the days the brine stands in the final pond – and that is set by a judgement about when to lift, which nobody records: “nothing at Aveste writes that part down.” B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the answer must fit all its parts.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1 lists what the mark sets out. Paragraph 2 reports Solbes’s panels: they “separated nothing the mark regulates” but did separate dwell, the number of days the brine stood in the final pond. Paragraph 3 explains why the lath still matters: it leaves the timing free. Paragraph 4 gives Panek’s point that a mark must hold up for an inspector. Paragraph 5 ends on the lath that no panel in five seasons has managed to taste and the morning judgement that every panel can taste.

steps.title: Find the thread
steps.text: The text puts it briefly: “The mark protects the lath. What the lath protects is the morning.” The rules guard what can be seen and photographed; the salt depends on a decision that nobody writes down.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B covers both halves. A says that the panels overturned faith in hand tools, although the findings are not “an argument against the lath”; C makes the price the reason the craft survives; and D blames damage by the machine, which the text rules out, and says that chemistry cannot explain the difference, although magnesium tracks dwell.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The mark guards the visible tools, while the salt depends on a judgement nobody records. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: Solbes’s panels are the most striking part of the text, and they found that the lath made no difference to the taste.
distractors.why_wrong: Nothing was overturned. The text says that the findings are not “an argument against the lath”, and Solbes is careful to say so too. The lath still matters because it leaves the timing free (step 2), and the mark still guarantees it.

distractors.why_tempting: Salt that carries the mark does fetch about six times the price of the bagged industrial grade.
distractors.why_wrong: The price is reported as a fact, not as the reason the craft survives. The text never asks whether hand-raked salt would outlast machine-harvested salt.

distractors.why_tempting: The panels can pick out the machine-harvested salt of Pella Marsa.
distractors.why_wrong: The text rules out damage by the machine: “it is not that the harvester bruises the crystal.” And chemistry does track the difference that matters: salt lifted at three days “carried roughly a fifth less magnesium” than salt lifted at eight.

p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For main-idea questions, look for a short sentence that sums up the whole text – here “The mark protects the lath. What the lath protects is the morning.” – and choose the option that says the same.
p5-elf-b13-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: An option can sound dramatic and still be wrong. A says that the panels overturned something, but Solbes is careful to say that the findings are not an argument against the lath.

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The guides tried to replace the handshake with the nod and the raised palm. To put something away as finished is to consign it to the past, so “consigned the handshake to the past” fits. The answer is C.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “Every guide to the new etiquette ___ the handshake to the past.” Etiquette is the set of rules for polite behaviour.

steps.title: Find the expression
steps.text: The next sentence describes a campaign against the handshake: cards “went up in lift lobbies”, and “the nod and the raised palm were drilled into staff at induction”. The guides set out to put the handshake away as finished. English says that something is consigned to the past when it is treated as over and done with.

steps.title: Check the other verbs
steps.text: To assign is to give someone a task or a place, or to say where something belongs. To design is to plan or make something. To resign is to give up a job, and to be resigned to something is to accept it unwillingly. None of them means putting the handshake away as finished.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Every guide to the new etiquette consigned the handshake to the past.” The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: “Assigned” looks very like the key, and it can be followed by “to”, as when a task is assigned to someone.
distractors.why_wrong: To assign is to give a task or a place, or to say where something belongs. The guides did more than place the handshake: they set out to get rid of it, with cards in the lobbies and new greetings drilled into staff (step 2). That is the meaning of “consigned … to the past”.

distractors.why_tempting: “Illustrated cards” went up in lift lobbies, so a word about design seems to belong.
distractors.why_wrong: To design is to plan or make something. The guides did not make the handshake; they tried to put it away as finished (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Resigned” looks like the key, and people are often said to be resigned to something.
distractors.why_wrong: To resign is to give up a job, and to be resigned to something is to accept it unwillingly. The guides were not accepting anything; they set out to put the handshake away as finished (step 2).

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a gap is followed by an object and a phrase such as “to the past”, look for the verb that forms an expression with them – here consign something to the past.
p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: All four options end in -signed, so the look of the word gives nothing away. Test each one in the whole frame, with “the handshake to the past”, not just with the word after the gap.

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: The sentence before says that the new greetings worked “for a season or two”. The gapped sentence goes against that: “the hand came back”. A sentence that goes against what was just said needs a contrast word, “Yet”. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap opens the short sentence “___ the hand came back.” The sentence before ends: “and for a season or two the drill held.”

steps.title: Find the relationship
steps.text: The drill held for a while; then the handshake returned. The second fact goes against what the first led you to expect, so the gap needs a contrast word: “Yet”, meaning but, all the same. The figures that follow confirm the return: four in five first meetings “still opened with one”.

steps.title: Check the other connectives
steps.text: “Likewise” means in the same way, “Besides” adds a further point in the same direction, and “Thus” marks a result. None of them shows that the handshake’s return goes against the drill’s success.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “Yet the hand came back.” The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Likewise” links two sentences smoothly, so it can sound right at the start of a sentence.
distractors.why_wrong: “Likewise” brings in something that happens in the same way. The hand coming back is not like the drill holding; it is the opposite (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Besides” is a common way to add a point.
distractors.why_wrong: “Besides” adds a point in the same direction. The return of the hand goes against the drill that held “for a season or two” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Thus” sounds formal and links one event to the next.
distractors.why_wrong: “Thus” marks a result, but the drill holding did not cause the handshake to come back. The two facts stand against each other (step 2).

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-002.technique: For a connective gap, ask whether the gapped sentence follows from the one before or goes against it. When something that worked “for a season or two” then fails, a contrast word fits.
p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: Short sentences can hide the logic. Read the sentence before the gap and decide the relationship before you look at the options.

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: If you refuse an offered hand, you still have to give a reason. What you owe someone after acting in a way they did not expect is an explanation. The answer is A.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “To decline one is still to owe a small ___, which is a strange burden to hang on a greeting”. To decline a handshake is to refuse it.

steps.title: Find the meaning
steps.text: Refusing an offered hand calls for a word or two of reason – a small explanation. English often says that you owe someone an explanation when you have done something they did not expect. The clause after the gap calls this duty “a strange burden to hang on a greeting”.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: An exclamation is a sudden cry or shout. An exploration is a search through a place or a subject. An expectation is something you think will happen. None of them is something you owe after refusing a hand.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: To decline a handshake “is still to owe a small explanation”. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: “Exclamation” looks very like the key.
distractors.why_wrong: An exclamation is a sudden cry. Refusing a hand does not leave you owing a cry; it leaves you owing a reason (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Exploration” has the same shape as the key: ex- at the start and -ation at the end.
distractors.why_wrong: An exploration is a search through a place or a subject. Nobody owes a search after turning down a handshake (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Greetings come with expectations, so the word seems to fit the topic.
distractors.why_wrong: An expectation is what someone thinks will happen. You may fail to meet someone’s expectation, but refusing a hand does not make you owe one; it makes you owe a reason (step 2).

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-003.technique: When a gap follows a verb such as “owe”, ask what is normally owed in that situation. After refusing something that is offered, people owe a reason.
p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: All four nouns look alike, with ex- at the start and -ation at the end. Do not choose by shape; choose the one that makes sense after “owe a small”.

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: “Seldom” turns the gap round: the moment is hardly ever what the gap says. Most people call it “a small test they are glad to have passed”, which shows some worry, and the next sentence says that this is “not the language of a comfortable ritual”. So the moment is seldom untroubled. The answer is B.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “The moment they describe is seldom ___”. Seldom means hardly ever, so the gap names what the moment hardly ever is.

steps.title: Use the evidence
steps.text: After the colon, the people describe the moment: “most call it a small test they are glad to have passed, and a few admit to having rehearsed it beforehand.” A test that you are glad to have passed causes a little worry. The next sentence confirms it: “That is not the language of a comfortable ritual but of something with stakes”, that is, something that can go well or badly. So the moment is hardly ever free of worry: it is seldom untroubled.

steps.title: Check the other adjectives
steps.text: “Seldom troubled” would mean usually calm, the opposite of the evidence. “Seldom unrehearsed” would mean nearly always rehearsed, but only “a few” admit to rehearsing. Uneventful means that nothing much happens; most people describe how the moment feels, not what happens in it.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: “The moment they describe is seldom untroubled”: it nearly always carries a little worry. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The sentence mentions rehearsing, so a word about rehearsal seems to match.
distractors.why_wrong: “Seldom unrehearsed” would mean that nearly everyone rehearses. The text says only that “a few admit to having rehearsed it beforehand” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A moment with stakes sounds eventful, so “seldom uneventful” can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: Uneventful means that nothing much happens. But most people describe how the moment feels – “a small test they are glad to have passed” – and the next sentence sets “a comfortable ritual” against “something with stakes”. That contrast is about ease and worry, which “untroubled” names (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The people describe worry, so a word for worry seems to match.
distractors.why_wrong: “Seldom” turns the word round: “seldom troubled” would mean that the moment is usually calm, which is the opposite of what most people say (step 2).

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a gap follows “seldom”, the gap names the opposite of what is usually true. Decide what the evidence shows, then pick the word that “seldom” turns into that meaning.
p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: The worried mood pulls towards “troubled”. But “seldom” reverses the word, so the right answer is its opposite, “untroubled”.

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: A hand “has to be met or refused, and either way an answer now exists”, and the sentence sets the handshake against “unfinished exchanges”. So the handshake finishes the first half-second. To finish something is to bring it to a close. The answer is D.

steps.title: Read the frame
steps.text: The gap sits in “the handshake brings the first half-second of an encounter to a ___”. An encounter is a meeting.

steps.title: Find the clue
steps.text: Just before, a nod “asks nothing and settles nothing”, while “A hand once out has to be met or refused, and either way an answer now exists.” After the gap, the working day is “made largely of unfinished exchanges”. So the handshake finishes something. English says that something is brought to a close when it is ended.

steps.title: Check the other nouns
steps.text: A clause is part of a sentence or of a contract. A course is a route, or a series of lessons. A cause is a reason, or an aim that people work for. None of them means an end, which the contrast with “unfinished exchanges” needs.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The handshake “brings the first half-second of an encounter to a close”. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: “Clause” looks and sounds very like the key.
distractors.why_wrong: A clause is part of a sentence or of a contract. The sentence needs a word for an end, set against “unfinished exchanges” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: A meeting has a course, the way it goes, so the word can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: A course is a route or the way something develops. The point is that the handshake ends the moment: an answer “now exists”, unlike the unfinished exchanges of the working day (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: “Cause” has almost the same letters as the key.
distractors.why_wrong: A cause is a reason, or an aim that people work for. The handshake does not turn the moment into a reason; it finishes it (step 2).

p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-005.technique: Use what comes after the gap as well as before it. Here “unfinished exchanges” shows that the gap means the opposite: an end, a close.
p5-elf-b13-002-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: All four nouns look alike: clause, course, cause, close. Only one goes with “brings … to a” and means an end.

p5-elf-b13-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: Ojala says that a generous radius “mostly buys tolerance”, and the next sentence explains: it spreads the load so that “a poor finish, a stray scratch, or a rivet set a millimeter off no longer decides how long the panel lives.” So the main benefit is that rough work no longer decides a panel’s life. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that you must work the answer out from what the text says. The question asks what the text implies about the rounded corners of cabin windows.

steps.title: Find the usual account
steps.text: The text opens with the usual reason: a hole in a pressurised tube is “a place where the load has to travel around something. That is why the corners are rounded”. But the panels at Tarnhouse “make it less tidy”.

steps.title: Find the test result
steps.text: The collection’s fatigue rigs – machines that load a panel over and over until it fails – have tested “skin panels cut by hand in the 1950s”, and the ones that failed first “were not the squarest: they were the ones whose edges the cutter had left rough, whatever the shape.”

steps.title: Find what the radius does
steps.text: Ojala says that a generous radius “mostly buys tolerance”, that is, room for small errors. It spreads the load so that a poor finish or a misplaced rivet “no longer decides how long the panel lives”. The last sentence makes the same point: square windows “were the way that left the shop floor no margin.” The shop floor is the part of a factory where the work is done.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C states this. A turns the usual idea into a rule that the test results go against, B says that hand-cut panels were given up, which the text never says, and D says that the tests could not confirm the usual account, although the explanation of the radius still rests on spreading the load.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Rounded corners mainly make a panel forgiving of rough work. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Most people know that rounded corners are safer, and A states that belief strongly.
distractors.why_wrong: The rig results go against it: the panels that failed first “were not the squarest” but those with rough edges, “whatever the shape” (step 3). Nothing in the text supports “always”.

distractors.why_tempting: The rigs showed that rough edges matter, so giving up hand cutting sounds like a sensible next step.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says what happened to hand cutting. The panels in the rigs were cut by hand in the 1950s, and the text reports only how they failed (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The panels “make it less tidy”, so the usual account can seem to have failed the test.
distractors.why_wrong: Making the account “less tidy” is not the same as failing to confirm it. The explanation of the result still rests on the load: a generous radius “spreads the load over enough metal” (step 4). The tests add to the usual account; the text never says that they failed to confirm it.

p5-elf-b13-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “implied” questions, put together what the text says about the thing named – here the rig results and what a generous radius “mostly buys” – and choose the option that follows from them without going further.
p5-elf-b13-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: An option that states a common belief strongly – here that a square window will “always” fail sooner – is a trap when the text’s evidence goes against it.

p5-elf-b13-004-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: The text sets the usual answer, that bread “dries out”, against what the institute found: a bagged loaf “loses almost no water overnight”, yet the tasters still mark it down. The text then explains why. The crumb stiffens, and the water it gives up moves out into the crust. “Nothing has left the bag; it has only moved.” B says this. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks for the point of the whole text, not a detail.

steps.title: Find the usual answer and the doubt
steps.text: The text opens with the common answer: bread goes stale because “it dries out”. The institute’s panels and scales “do not agree”: “A loaf sealed in a bag loses almost no water overnight, and the tasters still mark it down by morning”.

steps.title: Find the explanation
steps.text: “Two changes are running in opposite directions inside one loaf: the crumb stiffens as its starch settles back into an ordered form, and the water it gives up moves outwards and softens the crust.” The crumb is the soft inside of the bread. The text sums it up: “Nothing has left the bag; it has only moved.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B states the main point: staling moves water around inside the loaf rather than losing it. A is about keeping a crust crisp, which the text never discusses; C invents a disagreement between the tasters and the scales; and D runs both changes the wrong way.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about staling as water moving inside a loaf, not leaving it. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does describe a bagged crust that has gone limp.
distractors.why_wrong: The limp crust is evidence for the text’s point, not its subject. The text never discusses how to keep a crust crisp (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The tasters and the scales are both named near the start.
distractors.why_wrong: They are on the same side: both go against the idea that bread dries out. The scales show almost no water lost, and the tasters still mark the loaf down (step 2). There is no disagreement between them.

distractors.why_tempting: D describes water moving between the crust and the crumb, as the text does.
distractors.why_wrong: D runs both changes the wrong way. The water “moves outwards and softens the crust”, and the crumb “stiffens” (step 3); it does not go on softening.

p5-elf-b13-004-r1-ELF-001.technique: For main-idea questions on a short text, look for a sentence that sums up the point – here “Nothing has left the bag; it has only moved.” – and choose the option that says the same in other words.
p5-elf-b13-004-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: An option can use all the right words and still get the direction wrong. Check which way the water moves and what happens to the crumb.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: “Wear is not spread evenly along the chain either. It gathers in the length that sweeps the ground and in the two or three links either side of the swivel”. B says this in other words. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about wear on the mooring chain, the chain that holds a buoy to the seabed. The wear is described in paragraph 2.

steps.title: Find the wear sentence
steps.text: “Wear is not spread evenly along the chain either. It gathers in the length that sweeps the ground and in the two or three links either side of the swivel”. A swivel is a joint that lets the chain turn; here it sits above the sinker, the block of iron on the seabed.

steps.title: Add the detail about worn chains
steps.text: The text adds that “a chain condemned for losing a fifth of its diameter is usually condemned on a single bad metre.” A condemned chain is one judged unfit for use. So the wear is concentrated in a few places, not spread evenly along the chain.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B matches the two places. A spreads the loss over every link, C brings in salt corrosion, which the text never mentions, and D ties the wear to the inshore aids, which come up only in the argument about position.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Wear gathers where the chain sweeps the seabed and next to the swivel. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: “A fifth of its diameter” and the three-year cycle are both in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says the opposite of “Every link”: wear “is not spread evenly”, and a condemned chain “is usually condemned on a single bad metre” (steps 2 and 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Salt water does damage metal, so corrosion sounds like a likely cause.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions salt or corrosion. It names only where the wear gathers: in “the length that sweeps the ground” and next to the swivel (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Inshore aids and narrow water are both mentioned in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: They come up in the argument about how far buoys sit from their charted places: Cadell “concedes the inshore aids, where the water is narrow.” The text says nothing about wear being heavier inshore.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-001.technique: When a question asks what the text says about one thing, find the sentence about exactly that thing – here wear – and match the option to it. Watch for options that spread a local fact over everything.
p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: A uses two real figures from the text, a fifth and three years, but joins them into a claim that the text denies. Check how the figures are used, not just whether they appear.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: Wind and tide swing a buoy about its sinker, and “the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over, so the light is somewhere inside that circle rather than on the cross printed on the chart.” So a buoy away from its charted cross may simply have swung out on its chain, towards the edge of its circle. C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Implied” means that the answer is not stated outright. The question asks what follows when a buoy is found some way from its position on the chart.

steps.title: Find the slack mooring
steps.text: A floating aid “is moored, and a mooring has to be slack.” Chain longer than the depth lets the buoy rise with a wave instead of being pulled under. The ratio of chain to depth is called the scope.

steps.title: Find the circle
steps.text: “What scope costs is a circle: wind and tide swing the buoy about its sinker, and the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over, so the light is somewhere inside that circle rather than on the cross printed on the chart.” The sinker is the block of iron that holds the mooring to the seabed.

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: So a buoy found some way from its charted cross may just have swung out towards the edge of the circle its chain allows; its sinker need not have moved. Prigent’s loggers show this happening: through the spring tides, the buoys laid longest sit “as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places for hours together”.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C is this inference, worded with “may”. A turns buoy 43’s chain into a fixed rule, B reverses the link between chain and wander, and D invents an early lift.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: A buoy off its charted cross may simply be swinging out near the edge of its circle. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Buoy 43 has “thirty-one metres of it for eleven metres of water”, close to three to one.
distractors.why_wrong: That is one buoy, and the text treats scope as a choice: Cadell “lays his buoys long”, and buoy 43 goes back over the side “on the scope its master chose”. Nothing makes three to one a rule, and a figure for the chain does not say why a buoy is off its cross.

distractors.why_tempting: B sounds measured, and the text does link the chain to how far a buoy wanders.
distractors.why_wrong: B runs the link the wrong way. The text says “the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over” (step 3), and it is “the buoys laid longest” that sit as much as thirty-five metres from their places through the spring tides (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: A buoy out of place sounds like a problem that the crew would fix at once.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions early lifts. It says only that the district lifts each aid “once every three years”.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-002.technique: For “implied” questions, find the rule the text gives – here “the more chain it has, the wider the ground it can wander over” – and apply it to the case in the question. Keep the direction of the rule.
p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: B keeps the right words but turns the rule round. More chain means more wander, not less.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: The lightship’s logs carry three bearings every watch, “because a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it”. Fewtrell remembers: “We knew the shoal was under us” and “Where we were over it was another question.” So the problem of position is old. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks why the writer mentions the lightship: what job the paragraph does in the text.

steps.title: Find the ship’s record
steps.text: The lightship marked the shoal from 1911 until 1968. Its logs are “mostly weather”, but they also carry, “watch after watch, three bearings taken on the shore marks, because a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it.” A bearing is a direction measured to a fixed point, used to work out a position.

steps.title: Find Fewtrell’s memory
steps.text: Fewtrell, who served on the ship, remembers the mate chalking a corrected position by the companionway, and says: “We knew the shoal was under us” and “Where we were over it was another question.”

steps.title: Connect it to the rest
steps.text: Much of the text is about where buoys really sit: Prigent’s loggers, fitted since 2019, now put a figure on how far they wander. The lightship shows that the same uncertainty was known long before the loggers.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A names this job. B says that the lightship held its place better, although it moved too; C brings in a history of the whole coast that the text never gives; and D compares the old keepers with today’s crews, which the text never does.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The lightship shows that a marked position was uncertain long before the loggers. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: A ship with five men aboard sounds as if it could keep its place better than an empty buoy.
distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph stresses that the lightship moved too: “a moored ship does not sit still either” (step 2). It never claims that the lightship held its station better than a buoy does.

distractors.why_tempting: The text does say why this lightship was withdrawn.
distractors.why_wrong: It gives one reason for one ship: the harbour board set the cost of the crew against “a lamp on a hull that needed none”. The text never mentions a war or other manned stations.

distractors.why_tempting: The keepers took bearings watch after watch, which sounds very careful, and D is cautiously worded.
distractors.why_wrong: D is not why the writer brings the lightship in. The paragraph gives the reason for the bearings itself: “a moored ship does not sit still either and her keepers knew it” (step 2). The paragraph never mentions today’s crews, and the text never sets the keepers against them. When paragraph 4 says that the crews had only estimated the wander, it is showing what Prigent’s loggers added (step 4), not judging how closely anyone watched.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-003.technique: For “Why does the writer mention …” questions, ask what the paragraph adds to the main topic. Here much of the text is about where floating lights really sit, and the lightship shows that the question is an old one.
p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Do not answer with a detail of the paragraph, such as why the ship was withdrawn. The question asks what job the whole example does.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: “Cadell has read the recordings and concedes the inshore aids, where the water is narrow. On the outer stations he has not moved.” D says this. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about Cadell’s practice of laying buoys long, that is, on plenty of chain. Cadell’s practice is described in paragraph 4.

steps.title: Find Cadell’s reason
steps.text: Cadell argues that a buoy that rides easy comes through a February gale, while “a buoy moored short takes the sea in its chain rather than in the water, and it is the chain that fails.”

steps.title: Find Prigent’s figures
steps.text: Prigent’s loggers show that, through the spring tides, “the buoys laid longest sit as much as thirty-five metres from their charted places for hours together”, while small craft steer to the mark on the chart.

steps.title: Find Cadell’s answer
steps.text: “Cadell has read the recordings and concedes the inshore aids, where the water is narrow. On the outer stations he has not moved.” To concede is to admit that the other side is right on a point.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches the split. A says that Cadell has given the practice up, B gives a reason of cost that is not Cadell’s, and C says that the practice began after the storm, which the text never says.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: Cadell has given way on the inshore aids but not on the outer stations. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: Cadell did read the recordings, and the sentence goes straight on to a concession.
distractors.why_wrong: The concession is only partial: Cadell gives way on the inshore aids, but “On the outer stations he has not moved” (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: Cost is a natural argument in maintenance, and the text mentions cost elsewhere.
distractors.why_wrong: Cadell’s reason is about the sea, not price: a buoy moored short “takes the sea in its chain rather than in the water, and it is the chain that fails” (step 2). The text never compares the cost of chain with the cost of a buoy.

distractors.why_tempting: The two lost aids are real, and a storm sounds like a reason to change practice.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never says when Cadell began laying buoys long, and it never says that a storm made Cadell start. The two lost aids come up in the last paragraph, as a series “too thin” to show whether long moorings save buoys.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-004.technique: When a question asks about one person’s practice, read every sentence about that person to the end. A concession is often followed by a limit, as here: “On the outer stations he has not moved.”
p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Stopping at “concedes” leads to A. Read the next sentence, which limits the concession to the inshore aids.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The text follows a working morning on the Marram – the lift, the chain, the scope and the circle a buoy swings in – and sets Cadell’s long moorings against Prigent’s figures, leaving the question open: “Neither record disposes of the other.” B covers both parts. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the answer must fit all of it.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1 shows buoy 43 being lifted. Paragraph 2 explains moorings: why they must be slack, the circle a buoy swings in and where the chain wears. Paragraph 3 is about the old lightship. Paragraph 4 sets Cadell, who lays buoys long, against Prigent’s loggers. Paragraph 5 leaves the argument open, and buoy 43 goes back over the side.

steps.title: Find how it ends
steps.text: “Neither record disposes of the other.” To dispose of something is to deal with it for good. Here neither record proves the other wrong, so the question of how much chain to give stays open: “Prigent would like another ten years of loggers. Cadell would like a February.” Slack is the looseness of the chain.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B covers both the work of keeping floating lights in place and the open argument about slack. A makes the lightship the subject, C turns the loggers into a recommendation that the text never makes, and D brings in rising costs, which the text never discusses.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about keeping floating lights on station and an argument about slack that is still open. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The lightship has a whole paragraph of its own, with vivid memories.
distractors.why_wrong: It is one paragraph of five, used to show that position was uncertain long before the loggers. The rest of the text is about buoys, their chains and the argument over scope (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Prigent’s loggers give the text’s most precise figures, and Prigent would like another ten years of them.
distractors.why_wrong: The text reports what the loggers measured; it never argues that every aid should have one. Prigent would like “another ten years of loggers”, but the question is left open (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The cost of a crew is mentioned once, when the lightship was withdrawn.
distractors.why_wrong: That is a single reason for withdrawing one ship in 1968. The text never says that costs are rising, and it is about chains and positions, not budgets.

p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-005.technique: For main-idea questions on a long text, map each paragraph and look at how the text ends. If the text both describes something and reports a debate, the right option must cover both.
p5-elf-b14-001-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: A paragraph with vivid memories, like the lightship’s, is easy to remember and easy to overrate. Check how much of the text it really fills.

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-001.solution_path: “Four streets away, on a school converted the same year, a row of boxes in the same position on the same kind of gable fills most summers.” C says this. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what the text says about the boxes on the converted school. They appear in paragraph 1.

steps.title: Find the sentence
steps.text: “Four streets away, on a school converted the same year, a row of boxes in the same position on the same kind of gable fills most summers.” A gable is the triangular top of an end wall. Fills most summers means that bats use the boxes in most summers.

steps.title: See the contrast
steps.text: The laundry’s boxes have been up for eleven years, and “Not one of them has ever held a bat.” The text adds: “For a long time nobody at the borough could say what separated the two.”

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches. A turns “most summers” into every single summer, B gives fitting dates for these two rows that the text never gives, and D moves Talbourne’s three summers of logging to the school’s row.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The school’s row is used in most summers, in the same position as the laundry’s empty row. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: The school’s row works, so it is easy to remember it as always full.
distractors.why_wrong: The text says “most summers”, not every summer (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Oyelaran’s finding about boxes fitted in summer comes later, and it seems to explain the difference.
distractors.why_wrong: Oyelaran’s finding is about “most of the boxes that failed” across the borough; the text never gives the fitting dates of these two rows. It says that for a long time “nobody at the borough could say what separated the two” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does mention three summers of logging.
distractors.why_wrong: Those three summers belong to Talbourne’s own survey: Talbourne “spent three summers logging temperatures rather than counting animals”. The text never says that the school’s row was logged for three summers, or that any logging came before the planning conditions: Talbourne has surveyed roosts “since the conversions began”.

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-001.technique: For “What does the text say about …” questions, find the sentence about the thing named and keep its exact amounts – here “most summers”.
p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-001.pitfall: Details from later paragraphs, like the July fitting, can seem to explain an early sentence. Check whether the text really applies them to the thing the question names.

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-002.solution_path: By four in the afternoon the ridge end of the void can be ten or twelve degrees warmer than the eaves end, and Talbourne’s loggers show the animals “high and deep in the warm hours … out towards the cooler eaves at night.” D says this. The answer is D.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks what we are told about the roof voids. A roof void here is “the shallow, dusty gap between the slates and the boarding beneath them”.

steps.title: Find the temperatures
steps.text: “Slate heats quickly. By four in the afternoon the space near the ridge can stand at close to thirty degrees while the eaves end, shaded and open to the air, sits ten or twelve degrees below it, and by dawn the whole void has given its heat back.” The ridge is the top of the roof; the eaves are its lower edge.

steps.title: Find where the animals go
steps.text: “Talbourne's loggers show the animals working through that gradient: high and deep in the warm hours, when the young grow fastest, out towards the cooler eaves at night.” A gradient here is a range from warm to cool. High and deep means up near the ridge, the warm end in the afternoon.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: D matches: the warm end in the warm hours, the cool end at night. A reverses the movement, B brings in heat from the rooms below, which the text never mentions, and C keeps the afternoon difference until dawn, although by then the void “has given its heat back”.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The animals stayed high and deep, at the warm ridge end, in the warm hours, and moved out towards the cooler eaves at night. The answer is D.

distractors.why_tempting: It seems natural for animals to escape the heat in the day and seek warmth at night.
distractors.why_wrong: The loggers show the reverse: “high and deep in the warm hours … out towards the cooler eaves at night” (step 3). The text also notes that the warm hours are “when the young grow fastest”.

distractors.why_tempting: Heat rising from a building into its roof sounds like ordinary physics.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions heat from the rooms below. What warms the void is the roof itself: “Slate heats quickly.” And “by dawn the whole void has given its heat back” (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: The text does give a large difference between the two ends, ten or twelve degrees.
distractors.why_wrong: That difference is for four in the afternoon. By dawn “the whole void has given its heat back” (step 2), so the gap does not last until morning.

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-002.technique: When an option describes a movement through a day, check its direction against the text, hour by hour. Here the warm hours go with the ridge and the night with the eaves.
p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-002.pitfall: A follows common sense – shade in the heat, warmth at night – but runs the movement backwards. The text ties the warm hours to the young: they are “when the young grow fastest”.

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-003.solution_path: Cast boxes “held to three degrees or less”, but the two that were used “sat on a chimney breast whose flue still carried warm air up from the block's boiler”, and their loggers “recorded a swing much like the timber's”. So the range came from the warm flue, not from the box. A says this. The answer is A.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Suggest” means that the answer is not stated outright; you must put facts together. The question asks about the two cast boxes that bats used.

steps.title: Compare the two kinds of box
steps.text: In the trial, the timber boxes “moved about eleven degrees between afternoon and dawn”, and nine of the twelve were occupied within two summers. “The cast boxes held to three degrees or less, and two were used.” The cast boxes were made “in the same aggregate as the laundry's”: a stony mix poured into a mould.

steps.title: Find what was special about the two
steps.text: “Both of those two sat on a chimney breast whose flue still carried warm air up from the block's boiler, and the loggers inside them recorded a swing much like the timber's”. A flue is the pipe inside a chimney that carries hot air up. Cast boxes “on two other south-facing walls, with nothing behind them but insulation, stayed empty.”

steps.title: Draw the inference
steps.text: A cast box on its own held steady, but these two swung like timber. What the empty cast boxes on the other south-facing walls lacked was the warm flue behind them. So the swing came from the wall behind, not from the box.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: A is that inference. B says that the two were the only cast boxes on south-facing walls, although others on such walls stayed empty; C turns two boxes into a rule about sunny walls; and D says that their mix was thinner, although all the trial’s cast boxes used the laundry’s aggregate.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The warm flue, not the box, gave those two their range. The answer is A.

distractors.why_tempting: Sun on a south-facing wall seems likely to warm a box.
distractors.why_wrong: Cast boxes “on two other south-facing walls” stayed empty, so the two that were used were not the only cast boxes on such walls (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: Two cast boxes were used, so it can seem that cast boxes work under the right conditions.
distractors.why_wrong: The text never mentions how high the boxes hang, and a sunny wall was not enough: cast boxes on south-facing walls with only insulation behind them stayed empty (step 3). C draws a general rule that the text does not give.

distractors.why_tempting: A thinner material would heat and cool faster, so D sounds like a physical explanation.
distractors.why_wrong: The trial’s cast boxes were made “in the same aggregate as the laundry's” (step 2), and the text never mentions a thinner mix. What the two used boxes had was a warm flue behind them (step 3).

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-003.technique: For “suggest” questions, compare the cases that worked with those that did not and find the difference. Here the used cast boxes had a warm flue behind them, while the empty cast boxes on two other south-facing walls had only insulation.
p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-003.pitfall: Do not credit the box with what the wall behind it did. The cast material by itself held to three degrees or less.

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-004.solution_path: The writer says: “On the early boxes she was plainly right, and Talbourne says so.” But in the second series every box was fitted out of season, and timber still did far better than cast, so timing cannot explain that result. Right about the early boxes, not about the later series: that is C. The answer is C.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: The question asks for the writer’s attitude to Oyelaran’s objection. Keep the voices apart: Talbourne, Oyelaran and the writer.

steps.title: Find the objection
steps.text: Oyelaran “thinks the temperature account has been asked to carry more than it can.” The objection is about timing: most of the boxes that failed went up in June or July, and among the earliest boxes, those fitted between September and February “were taken up about three times as often as the summer ones.”

steps.title: Find what the writer grants
steps.text: The writer states plainly: “On the early boxes she was plainly right, and Talbourne says so.”

steps.title: Find what the writer does not grant
steps.text: Talbourne then chose to “hold the timing constant”: all twenty-four boxes were “fitted out of season”. Even so, nine of the twelve timber boxes were occupied within two summers, but only two of the twelve cast ones were used, both on a warm chimney breast. Timing cannot explain that split. The writer reports that Oyelaran “still holds that timing explains more of the whole record than he allows”, without taking that view.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: C matches: accepting as far as it goes. A says that the writer thinks material hardly matters at all, which the second series goes against; B says that the writer finds the file search too small, which the text never says; and D calls the writer dismissive, although the writer says that Oyelaran was “plainly right” about the early boxes.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The writer accepts the objection for the early boxes, but not for the later series. The answer is C.

distractors.why_tempting: Oyelaran’s line about the finest box standing empty in July is the most forceful in the text.
distractors.why_wrong: Neither the writer nor Oyelaran says that material hardly matters at all. Oyelaran’s line is about a box hung “in the middle of July”, and Oyelaran “accepts the second series”. When the timing was the same, the material did matter: nine of the twelve timber boxes were occupied within two summers, against two of the twelve cast ones (step 4).

distractors.why_tempting: B sounds measured, and the writer does not accept the objection in full.
distractors.why_wrong: The writer never questions the size of the file search. On the early boxes the writer calls Oyelaran “plainly right” (step 3).

distractors.why_tempting: The second series does limit the objection, so a negative option can seem to fit.
distractors.why_wrong: A writer who says that Oyelaran was “plainly right” about the early boxes is not dismissive (step 3). The writer calls the objection “documentary”, resting on the dates in the consent files, and the temperature record had not answered it: Talbourne needed a new series with the timing held constant (step 4).

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-004.technique: For attitude questions, find the sentence where the writer judges in the writer’s own voice – here “On the early boxes she was plainly right” – and then check how far the judgement reaches.
p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-004.pitfall: Two options are measured in tone. B and C both grant the objection something, but only C matches where the writer draws the line: the early boxes, not the later series.

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-005.solution_path: The text opens with two matched rows of bat boxes, one never used and one used in most summers, and says that for a long time “nobody at the borough could say what separated the two.” The rest follows the search for the answer: temperature range, timing and material. B names that question. The answer is B.

steps.title: Understand the question
steps.text: “Mainly about” asks about the whole text, so the answer must fit all its parts.

steps.title: Map the text
steps.text: Paragraph 1 sets the laundry’s empty boxes against the school’s row, which “fills most summers”. Paragraph 2 gives Talbourne’s account: in the roof voids the animals moved through a range of temperatures, and “where the choice is missing, they do not stay long.” Paragraph 3 gives Oyelaran’s objection about timing. Paragraph 4 reports the trial that held the timing constant. Paragraph 5 describes the new guidance and the laundry’s row, still in place.

steps.title: Find the thread
steps.text: Each part works on the question raised in paragraph 1: what separates the boxes that bats use from those they leave empty. A roost is a place where bats rest, so the boxes are purpose-built replacement roosts.

steps.title: Test the options
steps.text: B names that question. A makes planning conditions the subject, C says that Talbourne gave up counting animals altogether, and D invents a dispute about how much of a building to keep.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.text: The text is about why some replacement roosts are used while others stand empty. The answer is B.

distractors.why_tempting: The boxes went up under a planning condition, and the text ends with new guidance.
distractors.why_wrong: Planning is only the setting. The text’s question is why some boxes are used and others are not (step 3); it says nothing about planning conditions in general.

distractors.why_tempting: Talbourne did spend three summers “logging temperatures rather than counting animals”.
distractors.why_wrong: That was a choice of method for three summers, not a decision to stop counting “altogether”, and a method is not the subject of the text (step 2).

distractors.why_tempting: Talbourne and Oyelaran do disagree, and Oyelaran is a building conservation officer.
distractors.why_wrong: Their disagreement is about why boxes stand empty – temperature or timing – not about how much of a building should be kept (step 2).

p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-005.technique: For main-idea questions, look for the question the text raises at the start – here what separated the two rows – and check that the option names it. The later paragraphs usually work on that question.
p5-elf-b14-003-r1-ELF-005.pitfall: A setting is not a subject. Planning conditions frame the story, but the text is about which boxes bats use.
